title: EU and NAFTA/USMCA

cards.b:
Regionalisation means states in a region cooperating more closely, in trade, money or even politics. The two biggest examples in the West are very different.

  • The European Union is the deepest integration project in history: a single market, a common currency for 21 states, shared laws and a parliament.
  • NAFTA (1994), replaced by the USMCA (2020), is a free trade agreement among the US, Canada and Mexico, with no supranational bodies.

UPSC asks you to compare them, explain the EU's institutions and crises, and assess what changed from NAFTA to USMCA. The topic links to functionalism, globalisation and India's own FTAs (India-EU, concluded 2026).

Bela Balassa's The Theory of Economic Integration (1961) set out the ladder.

  • Free trade area: no tariffs among members; each keeps its own external tariff (NAFTA/USMCA, SAFTA).
  • Customs union: plus a common external tariff (EU since 1968, Mercosur).
  • Common market: plus free movement of labour and capital.
  • Economic and monetary union: plus a common currency and policies (eurozone).
  • Political union.

Jacob Viner (1950) showed that integration can create trade or divert it from cheaper outsiders.

• 1951 ECSC; 1957 Treaties of Rome (EEC); 1968 customs union.
  • Enlargements: UK, Ireland, Denmark (1973); Greece (1981); Spain, Portugal (1986); Austria, Finland, Sweden (1995); ten states mostly from Central and Eastern Europe (2004); Bulgaria, Romania (2007); Croatia (2013).
  • 1986 Single European Act; 1992 Maastricht (EU, citizenship, euro plan, three pillars); 1997 Amsterdam; 2001 Nice; 2007 Lisbon (in force 2009: legal personality, permanent European Council President, High Representative, citizens' initiative, Article 50 exit clause).
  • 1995 Schengen in force; 1999 euro launched; 2002 notes and coins.
  • 2020 UK left (the only exit so far).
  • 2026: Bulgaria became the 21st euro member on 1 January.

Candidate states include Ukraine and Moldova (status 2022), the Western Balkans and Turkiye (talks frozen). Montenegro and Albania are seen as the front-runners.

• European Commission (Brussels): proposes laws, enforces treaties, negotiates trade. One commissioner per state. President: Ursula von der Leyen (second term from 2024).
  • European Council: heads of state or government; sets direction. President: Antonio Costa (from December 2024).
  • Council of the EU: national ministers; co-legislator. Most votes by qualified majority (55% of states with 65% of population); unanimity on foreign policy and tax.
  • European Parliament: directly elected since 1979; 720 members after the 2024 election; co-legislator.
  • Court of Justice of the EU: supremacy and direct effect of EU law (Van Gend en Loos, 1963; Costa v ENEL, 1964).
  • European Central Bank (Frankfurt): monetary policy for the eurozone.

The EU mixes supranational (Commission, Court, ECB, Parliament) and intergovernmental (European Council) features. Scholars call it a sui generis polity.

• Democratic deficit: distant institutions and low turnout.
  • Eurozone crisis (2010-12): Greek debt, bailouts, austerity; ECB's Mario Draghi pledged "whatever it takes" (2012).
  • Migration crisis (2015) and the 2024 Pact on Migration and Asylum.
  • Brexit (2016 vote; exit 31 January 2020).
  • Rule of law disputes with Hungary and Poland; funds were withheld.
  • Populism and Eurosceptic parties grew in the 2024 elections.
  • War in Ukraine (2022): sanctions, energy shift from Russia, and a defence push (ReArm Europe, 2025).
  • Trade pressure from US tariffs in 2025-26 and from Chinese competition.

Yet each crisis has also produced more integration: the NextGenerationEU recovery fund (2020) with joint borrowing, and joint defence spending. Jean Monnet's line that Europe would be forged in crises is often cited.

The North American Free Trade Agreement came into force on 1 January 1994. It built on the 1988 Canada-US FTA.

  • Removed most tariffs among the US, Canada and Mexico over 15 years.
  • Covered investment (with investor-state dispute settlement, Chapter 11), services and intellectual property.
  • Side agreements on labour and environment.
  • Dispute panels on trade remedies (Chapter 19).

Effects. Trade among the three grew several times over. Integrated supply chains, especially in cars, crossed borders many times. Mexico gained factories (maquiladoras) but rural farmers suffered from cheap US corn. US critics blamed it for lost manufacturing jobs; economists found modest net effects. The Zapatista uprising in Chiapas began the day NAFTA took effect.

Donald Trump called NAFTA "the worst trade deal". Renegotiation produced the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (Canada calls it CUSMA, Mexico T-MEC), signed on 30 November 2018 and in force on 1 July 2020.

Key changes

  • Cars: regional value content raised to 75%, and 40-45% of a car made by workers earning at least $16 an hour.
  • Labour: Mexico reformed union laws; a rapid-response mechanism targets factories.
  • Digital trade chapter; longer patent and copyright terms.
  • ISDS largely removed for Canada and limited for Mexico.
  • A "non-market economy" clause aimed at China.
  • Sunset clause: a 16-year term with a joint review after six years.

• In 2025 the US placed tariffs on Canada and Mexico, citing fentanyl and migration, but exempted goods that met USMCA rules. Steel, aluminium and car tariffs (Section 232) hit both partners.
  • The first joint review fell on 1 July 2026. The US declined to extend the agreement in its current form. That triggers annual reviews; the deal remains in force until 2036 unless all three agree to extend. Any party may withdraw with six months' notice.
  • US-Mexico talks have covered car rules of origin, steel and economic security. Canada's talks lagged.
  • New US Section 301 tariffs from July 2026 exclude USMCA-compliant goods.

The lesson: a free trade area without strong institutions is vulnerable to the power of its largest member. Check the latest before the exam.

Depth

EU: customs union, single market, euro, common law. USMCA: free trade area only.

Institutions

EU: supranational Commission, Parliament and Court. USMCA: a Free Trade Commission of ministers and dispute panels.

Power

EU: several big states balance each other. USMCA: one dominant member (the US) with about 85% of the combined GDP.

Goals

EU: peace and political union. USMCA: commerce and supply chains.

Theory

EU fits neofunctionalism and liberal intergovernmentalism; USMCA fits realist and hegemonic models.

cards.h: India, the EU and North America
cards.b:
• EU. India's largest or second-largest trading partner in goods. Strategic partnership since 2004. The India-EU FTA was concluded on 27 January 2026 after talks that began in 2007; separate investment and geographical-indications deals were negotiated. The EU-India Trade and Technology Council was set up in 2022-23. Friction points: the EU's carbon border tax (CBAM) and its deforestation rules.
  • US. India's largest export market. Tariffs on Indian goods rose to 50% in 2025, then an interim framework in February 2026 aimed at 18%. Status is evolving.
  • Canada. Ties fell sharply in 2023-24 over the Nijjar case and began to thaw in 2025.
  • Mexico is a growing partner in cars and pharma.
  • Lessons for India: the EU shows the value of institutions; USMCA shows the risks of dependence on one market. India prefers FTAs to deep integration.

"Compare the European Union with NAFTA/USMCA as models of regional integration."
"Is the EU facing a crisis of integration?"

Structure: define regionalisation; Balassa's stages diagram. EU: growth, institutions, crises, resilience. NAFTA: aims and effects. USMCA: changes and the 2026 review. Comparison table. India's links: India-EU FTA, US tariffs.
